title: Questions about grad sessions

questions.q: Can we bring things that actually matter to them?
questions.a: Please do. A sport, an instrument, a uniform, ROTC or 4-H gear, medals, art, a gaming setup, the truck they saved up for, a horse, a career-tech project. A senior session should look like this particular person's last year of high school, not like a template with their face in it.

questions.q: My senior is awkward in front of a camera. Now what?
questions.a: Most of them are, at first. I show a few ideas, they tell me what feels right and what feels ridiculous, and I talk them through it from behind the camera. I'll show them the back of the camera along the way so they can see it's going fine. I never physically move anyone into a pose.

questions.q: How many outfits can they bring?
questions.a: Roughly one for a Short session, one or two for a Standard, and two to four for an Extended, which also gives us room for a second nearby setting as time allows.
I have a pop-up changing tent I can bring for sessions with multiple looks. Say so ahead of time and I'll have it with me.

questions.q: The senior and I want different things. Who wins?
questions.a: Both of you, usually. Seniors tend to want images that feel like them — a bit more personality, a bit more attitude. Parents usually want something timeless for announcements and for the relatives. Those aren't in conflict; they just need a few minutes of planning so we get both while we're out there.
Whatever reflects them, in clean shoes. Accessories are welcome — a hat, a scarf, sunglasses, a jersey. Avoid big logos unless the logo is the point.
